speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Trains reigned supreme until the emergence of automobiles and airplanes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Electricity replaced kerosene as our energy source for light.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Steel outmuscled iron, bricks and mortar to allow us to build superstructures such as skyscrapers and bridges over large bodies of water.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Each and every time this happened, incumbent industries suffered and new ones boomed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is the cycle of technology and business.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Just the other day, I read of Netflix's US$105 million purchase of Martin Scorsese's new gangster film starring Robert De Niro named "The Irishman".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I must confess that I did not know what Netflix was.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As usual, when it comes to technology, my daughters had to educate their father about how I can now watch award-winning TV shows, movies and documentaries, on-demand, via streaming through the Internet for a reasonably small subscription fee.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Through large volume subscriptions, Netflix now has the resources to compete with traditional movie production houses and even begin production of movies and shows of their own.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Locally, I understand that Netflix is fast gaining popularity amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: What does this mean for cable television providers, such as StarHub and Singtel?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Netflix has the latest content, with easy on-demand access, at a cost lower than cable television or movie theatres.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: While it is too early to tell what will happen next in the movie/TV entertainment industry, what we do know is that business can no longer be conducted "as usual" in the industry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Netflix's entry into the movie/TV entertainment industry is not unlike the entry of private hire cars into the point-to-point transportation industry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire car companies made their foray into Singapore in 2013.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Of these, Uber and Grab now constitute the largest market share.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A key reason for the rapid growth of private hire car services in Singapore is their ability to address the perennial complaint of Singapore commuters − the difficulty of getting taxis during peak hours, in remote areas and during inclement weather.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is despite Singapore having one of the highest taxis-to-population ratios in the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire car companies are able to plug this service gap through their mobile apps which provide a platform to efficiently match private hire car drivers and passengers directly in real time and space.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Acting as a marginal supplier, private hire car drivers come onto the road readily to soak up latent demand as and when required.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This significantly shrinks transaction costs, giving passengers greater choices and value.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Taxi drivers facing increased competition were naturally displeased.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They argue that taxis have to adhere to a fixed schedule of charges and comply with availability requirements.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There was a daily minimum mileage that taxi drivers needed to clock and a specified number of taxis need to ply the streets during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This makes them inflexible in pricing and uncompetitive against private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There were, initially, also no regulatory requirements for anyone to be an Uber or Grab driver.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: All you needed was a driving licence and a car.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire car drivers were not required to apply for or take any tests to obtain a vocational licence.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Uber and Grab used technology as leverage to match demand with supply and reduced transaction costs considerably to capture a significant portion of the point-to-point transportation market.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire cars tripled its numbers on our roads in as many years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire car drivers, on the other hand, point to exclusive advantages that taxis enjoy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Taxis are allowed to pick up passengers who hail them on the streets.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Taxis also enjoy exemption from the child seat rule, which mandates that all children under 1.35 metres in height are required to be in a child seat when travelling in a car.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: All the above issues have been well-aired in the mass media.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Should the Government support the plea from some taxi drivers to ban private hire cars in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Or should the Government adopt a laissez-faire approach and allow the free market to regulate itself?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Government picked an answer somewhere in between.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, the Government did not step in nor interfered directly with the disruption that technology has caused in the point-to-point transportation industry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Uber and Grab were filling a demand and consumers were, ultimately, benefiting from wider choices at better value.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, recent trends suggest that the industry, on the whole, may have benefited from the disruption.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A larger "pie" means that the industry can sustain both taxis and private hire cars, while consumers continue to enjoy the best of both worlds at better value.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is a positive sign for commuters and the industry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: New technologies will always disrupt stable, entrenched industries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is clear from past and present examples.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Stifling new innovative technology can only end in a negative outcome for the overall Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I had said in my Budget Debate speech that I empathised with taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These policies have objectives designed for the collective good.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: How do we take full advantage of new technologies in order to ensure that our economy remains nimble, vibrant and on the cutting-edge and still ensure that no one is left behind?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, reliability of our train systems should be a major focus of the Government as it had done in recent times.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will help us enhance the reliability of trains and tracks from contributing to breakdowns.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One other issue that concerns estates, such as the new BTOs of Keat Hong Pride and Crest in my constituency, is that they are not covered by noise barriers today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Trains on the North-South line increase in frequency due to signalling enhancements and, quite often, you can also hear trains travelling towards depots past midnight.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many residents are impacted by the level of noise from the tracks and trains.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents have complained that the noise from concrete sleepers is much louder, compared to the old wooden ones.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NEA has set acceptable noise levels in decibels.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can I ask if this is a determining factor and what is the acceptable decibel level for LTA to put in place noise barriers?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In our current situation, it does seem that LTA has put the responsibility on HDB to put in place noise mitigation measures, and we seem to be going in circles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If, indeed, the decibel levels are equivalent or higher compared to the areas that have benefited from noise barriers, such as those that are being implemented just 100 metres to 200 meters along the current track, then the decision to implement noise barriers should be quite clear-cut.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: LTA needs to be transparent in the criteria to implement noise barriers which, currently, is not clear to the public.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In recent years, MOT has done a significant job in reducing MRT breakdowns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These unfortunate incidents often occurred during the peak hours, affecting thousands of Jurong residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Are there plans to improve the train reliability between these two stations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Or would it be helpful to increase the engineering hours to fix the problems?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope the Minister can look at this seriously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfortunately, I have to repeat the cut again this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Contrary to recent survey findings, train breakdowns and delays have been happening so frequently that commuters are getting increasingly frustrated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems like train faults are becoming the norm for us now, which is not where we want our Singapore transport system to go.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I have said at the COS last year, Singaporeans should not have to get used to this regularity of disruptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should expect our system to have far fewer disruptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the Ministry's plans to improve the situation and will commuters see a significant decrease in the number of train delays, faults or disruptions this year?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Low Yen Ling, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This uptake in public transport has come on the back of the Government's efforts to improve connectivity, with the addition of the Downtown Line, as well as more buses and trains.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While more Singaporeans are enjoying better public transport options and higher commuter satisfaction, some 5,600 residents living in the Hume area are still being held back by low train and bus connectivity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This stretch is more than double the average 1.1 km distance found between most MRT stations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, Hume residents have little choice but to make their way to Hillview or Beauty World MRT stations via a detour and crowded buses.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I sincerely appeal to MOT and LTA to review the merits of opening Hume MRT station.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Hillview and Hume resident population is set to increase further with the addition of more condominium projects to the current 20 over condominiums present in that belt.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, the upcoming Rail Corridor development will certainly bring greater human and motor traffic to the area.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The masterplan will create an attractive residential and community oasis.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With eight distinctively themed stretches along its 24 kilometres, the Rail Corridor will attract nature lovers, history buffs, cyclists, runners, families and even tourists who wish to experience Singapore's history in a new way.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Rail Corridor is the legacy of the Singapore-Malaya rail link that started in 1903.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In its vicinity is the gallery "Surviving the Japanese Occupation: War and its Legacies".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The confluence of rich history, greenery and recreational opportunities makes it a unique experience and attraction that can enhance tourism and boost Singaporeans' appreciation of our historical and green heritage.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, without train connectivity for easy access by the masses, these treasures that I talked about may remain the enjoyment of those with vehicles, limiting its potential and pull for the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: May we know if MOT will support the development of the Rail Corridor as well as the anticipated rise of human and motor traffic to the area with an MRT station in Hume?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how will LTA and MOT help Hillview and Hume residents gain greater satisfaction in public transport, especially in train connectivity?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With easy access via a Hume MRT station, we hope all of Singapore will get to appreciate what the area has to offer.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is certainly a move that will be welcomed by all residents in Hume and Hillview.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We would like to thank and commend them for their efforts.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We appreciate the recent addition of bus number 973 last month.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is connecting the areas between Bukit Panjang, Hillview Avenue and Hume Avenue.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are grateful for City Direct bus number 653 that has made it easier for Hillview and Hume residents to get to and from the CBD area at peak hours.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many residents have told me that because of the convenience and comfortable ride on bus number 653, they now leave their cars at home on weekdays.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These improvements are moving us nearer the vision of a green and car-lite Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With new train lines and more public buses, more Singapore residents are taking public transport to work.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a rise of 4% from the year 2010.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We certainly want to encourage such commuter behaviour.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we still face some bus connectivity challenges in Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, to get to Hillview MRT station, our Hume residents need to backtrack in their bus routes, and buses are always packed during peak hours.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those going to the city via the Beauty World MRT station are often subject to a long wait because most buses plying Upper Bukit Timah Road are full by the time they reach Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many residents report waiting 15 minutes or even more before boarding a bus.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the new bus 973 can only stop 200 metres ahead of Hillview MRT Station instead of the bus stop just outside the Hillview MRT station, because of the bus route.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I want to reaffirm my thanks and gratitude to the LTA team for working hand-in-hand with us.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There has been much progress but in terms of offering a good "first-and-last-mile" experience, we do still have room for improvement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to addressing these commuting blues, we hope the authorities can look ahead to provide good bus connectivity for Bukit Gombak residents to get to their new and upcoming Community Club at Hillview Avenue.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, the location is under-served in terms of access to the MRT stations of Hillview, Bukit Gombak and Beauty World.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We estimate about half of residents in the constituency do not have public transport connections to the Community Club, which is scheduled to open later this year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Community Club will be a central node of many activities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Among its many new features are a childcare centre, culinary school and rooftop garden.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, easy access by public transport is vital for Bukit Gombak residents to access these amenities and for community bonding.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will certainly encourage more residents to join in the movement for Singapore to become car-lite and green.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our Minister has been talking about a car-lite society, and I am all for it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To be car-lite, we need to further improve our public transport.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make bus journeys, especially in the morning and evening peak hours, more pleasant.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But for many Nee Soon South residents, this is not the case.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They have to travel north and come back south again, and then go to Khatib.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A good public transport service should also cater to the residents living in private estates as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also ask for covered linkways from the back gates of the condominiums to the nearest bus stop to improve accessibility, so that they, too, can enjoy taking public transport.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have put up requests for two condominiums, The Estuary and Forest Hill, and I hope this Budget will have good news for my residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, a sheltered linkway along Yishun Avenue 2 to the Yishun Sports Complex would also bring plenty of cheer to the residents on a rainy day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It will be a perfect place to call home if our Transport Minister can have his magic touch to our bus services.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Melvin Yong, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is evident as commuters' satisfaction in public transport had climbed to a nine-year high in 2016.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Consequently, our bus captains carry the responsibility of fulfilling these standards every day, and it is important that we give them our fullest support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, bus captains are required to abide by specific arrival timings at bus stops.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bus captains also tell me there is an increase in the number of bus stops now designated as checkpoints, where they must meet specified timing requirements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, narrow ingress and egress points at bus interchanges, traffic conditions and even weather conditions can adversely affect the arrival timings.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry review these timing requirements and the number of checkpoints to allow for some form of flexibility, considering bus operations are subjected to unpredictable road and weather conditions that are often not within the drivers' control?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, the running time for bus captains to complete their bus journey should be reviewed to accommodate peak and non-peak periods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, our Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) rates are reviewed quarterly by LTA to take into account peak and non-peak periods like school holidays.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With data analysis, I hope LTA can review and adjust the bus running time in a similar fashion.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Commuters have complained that they do not understand why buses travel slowly even when there are no vehicles ahead.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many do not know that our bus captains need to meet the service timings.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can LTA work with the union to raise public awareness on these service requirements under the Bus Contracting Model (BCM)?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under this programme, we have seen an injection of more buses over the past years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the current infrastructure, particularly the older bus interchanges, were not expanded to cope with the increase in buses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bus captains now need to wait longer for available bus parking lots, which affect their already-short layover time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, ground feedback indicates that information on the CFMS used by the Bus Operations Centre Controllers is not always synchronised accurately with the Driver Display Unit (DDU) used by our bus captains in the bus.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This means that the CFMS may show that bus captains are late reaching the bus stops, while their DDU in the bus shows otherwise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can LTA do more to improve the stability of these systems?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, we have heard of cases where bus captains are abused and even assaulted by commuters while performing their duty.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bus captains should not be distracted from driving the bus for the safety of the commuters on board and all road users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the union's part, we will work with the public bus operators to make a police report for every case of assault against our bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope investigations of such cases by the Police would be handled promptly and there should be strict prosecution of offenders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also hope that commuters understand that our bus captains work hard to bring us to our destinations safely and on time, every day and every night.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I ask for your support to ensure that they work in a safe environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many commuters depend on our public rail transport daily.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, they may be unaware of the hard work that our rail maintenance professionals put in − often behind the scenes − to keep our rail transportation running.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With more focus on rail reliability, as highlighted by several Members earlier, the role of our rail workers is more critical than before.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to uplift the profession and ensure that there is a consistent pipeline of talent into the industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, we must ensure that our rail workers can perform their duties in a safe environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, they battle challenging working conditions at the underground depot and poorly-ventilated tunnels.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More can be done to improve their work environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to ensure that the air conditions in the underground depot in our tunnels do not pose any health concerns for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, as technology continues to advance, our rail workers need to keep up with the changes and stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry share more about the Academy's training programmes?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we establish a Rail Manpower Development Plan to systematically build up our talent pool?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must be able to send our local talents to learn at the best foreign institutes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I hope that the Ministry can work with the union and our rail operators to raise public awareness on the important work of our rail workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would not only instil a sense of pride among our existing rail workers, but also help to attract future ones.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the move by the Ministry to exempt the contribution of motorcycles to a quota to the open COE category.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hopefully, this move may help to ease the motorcycle COE price dilemma.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe a more encompassing and inclusive measure can be introduced and implemented to regulate the motorcycle COE prices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If the COE for cars can be categorised in such a manner, why can it not be done for motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I still think it is one of the better ways to mitigate the issue of high motorcycle COE prices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, observers and commentators viewed the introduction of tiered ARF as being meant to mitigate the high motorcycle COE prices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Can I have the Minister's confirmation as this was not mentioned explicitly during Minister Heng's Budget Speech.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If the answer is yes, how can this be achieved and, if no, what is the actual purpose of this implementation?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, when implementing Government policies, blind spots often occur.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, problems will eventually be solved via effective communications between Government agencies and trade associations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Two years ago, during the Chamber's luncheon dialogue with representatives from the transport industry, the Singapore Motor Cycle Trade Association gave us the feedback that, as a result of the COE system, the quota for motorcycle COEs keeps being reduced.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We realised that motorcycle buyers actually fall under two categories.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: One category of buyers use motorcycles to make a living.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The other category of buyers use motorcycles for leisure activities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With a smaller quota, the COE would be driven up, and the impact would be acutely felt by those who depend on motorcycles for their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Motor Cycle Trade Association provided this feedback to Land Transport Authority, and SCCCI also helped to lobby by adding our views.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: LTA also announced that it would continue to seek feedback from the industry and public, so that the COE system could meet the demands of the population at large more equitably.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This case study shows that LTA has responded promptly to industry feedback and helped to solve their problems.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: SCCCI also engages in similar channels of communication with other Government agencies and, moving ahead, will help even more trade associations to provide constructive industry-related views.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First of all, I would like to comment about the recent changes in motorcycle COEs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Motorcyles are the lifeblood for many of our working class.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about light goods vehicles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses, especially SMEs operating light goods vehicles (LGVs), face many challenges today, and this contributes to high business transportation costs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In view of these challenges, I have a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the Traffic Police department, foreign worker drivers need to prove that they have a manual Class 3 driving licence, which is a near impossibility, given the countries they come from.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, they will be issued automatic Class 3 driving licence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, not having many manual transmission vehicles available for purchase is going to create real operational challenges for many companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Second, would MOT consider allowing LGV owners to renew their COEs with tenures equivalent to their remaining statutory lifespan, versus the current five-year mark, so as to reduce the cost and cash flow associated with the extended COEs?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Third, can the Early Turnover Scheme (ETS) hopefully, be enhanced as well as extended by increasing the current and upcoming discount on COEs for LGVs, similar to heavy goods vehicles (HGVs), and extending the ETS to include Euro 5 through perhaps lower incentives, and not just Euro 6 vehicles?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, can MOT consider delinking the COE supply contribution from commercial vehicle de-registrations to the Open Category, just like what has been announced for motorcycle COE whereby de-registrations from motorcycles will no longer contribute to Open Category COEs in the preceding quarter.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: There will be challenges, but we will be in a good position if we can succeed in capturing the many opportunities that will also arise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Budget 2017 calls on all stakeholders to work together to seize these opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The transport sector is a key pillar of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many Singaporeans make a good living working in it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The potential for further growth is also great.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many well-paying jobs are waiting to be filled.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: More importantly, the transport sector is a key enabler for our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It connects us not just within our island, but to the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This started from Singapore's early days as a centre for entrepot trade and allows Singapore to thrive as an international hub today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The transport sector is also a crucible of innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Who knows what else the future will bring?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Working with EDB, we offer Singapore as a test-bed, an incubator for new ideas, and for companies and start-ups to run trials here.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: What works can then be commercialised elsewhere and, along the way, we hope some local companies can acquire new capabilities and business opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Later, Second Minister Ng Chee Meng and Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo will elaborate on some of these exciting initiatives and trends.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many of these changes will happen during their career.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is appropriate for the young Ministers to spearhead these developments and see them through.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As for me, I shall look forward to enjoying the benefits as a consumer during my lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I agree with Mr Sitoh Yih Pin on the inevitability of technology advancements.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The human mind is wired to explore new ways of doing things.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And we will always seek to better our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Last week, DeepStack was reported to have beaten the world's best poker players, and we knew that artificial intelligence had already beaten chess grandmasters and Go champions several years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These technology advancements will create opportunities to change and improve our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If Netflix offers better value than Starhub TV, consumers will switch.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am familiar with Netflix, but I do not use it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I still enjoy going to the cinema, the old romantic ambience of the cinema.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is the hard reality of the market that incumbents will always suffer.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Such competition is unsettling for them, but it is good for consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As regulators, our job is not to stifle innovation but to be fair to all players, and we should always put consumer interest as our top priority.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But I agree with Mr Sitoh Yih Pin that as a Government, we should also be concerned about the workers who will be impacted.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: He highlighted the stress on the taxi drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We should help them, not by insulating them from innovations, but by alerting them to the potential disruption and preparing them for change.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Change is unpleasant but everyone can be helped to adapt to change.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As noted by the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE), the best way to ensure relevance is to acquire and develop deep skills, and going beyond that, to master competencies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong was there with me at the launch.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have great ambitions for the Rail Academy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It will develop programmes to train workers in critical areas of rail operations and maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It will work with the rail operators and the Institutes of Higher Learning to offer pre-employment programmes, as well as continuing education and training.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: An example is the part-time Diploma in Rapid Transit Technology.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I agree with Mr Melvin Yong that we should also learn from good rail operators overseas by attaching our professionals there to pick up best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Rail Academy will develop a competency framework for railway professionals and also accredit training programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Academy will also take charge of industry branding and work with industry partners to improve working conditions by utilising technology to lighten workloads and enhance employee health management.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: What is most critical is for our transport workers to be open to learning new skills.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Then, they can ride the wave of technological change.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I agree with Mr Melvin Yong that we must tap on the strong tripartite relationship and platforms to help our workers adjust.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For taxi drivers affected by competition, we are working with the National Taxi Association and taxi companies to help them cope.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For bus captains, we are working with the National Transport Workers' Union and the public bus operators to help them adapt.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Where these will lead us, we cannot be sure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But I think it sure will be exciting!

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have simplified the evolving drama under the banner of "Making Singapore Car-Lite by 2030".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But it is much more than about cars or their depopulation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is also about making it easier and more enjoyable for everyone to walk, cycle and take public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: There will be less need to own cars, and we can look forward to reclaiming many road lanes and car-park spaces and using them instead for the community and for greenery.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is about a lifestyle change, a mindset shift and improving the quality of life for all.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are testing many of these ideas in Ang Mo Kio by making it a model cycling town.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are making Tampines Town the second model walking and cycling town.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Today, many residents there already use bicycles and PMDs to get around.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many who work in Tampines live in adjacent towns, so we will provide trunk cycling routes, connecting Tampines to neighbouring towns and also to Changi Business Park and Singapore Expo.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will improve crossings, widen footpaths and improve safety at bus-stops.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are determined to make cycling and the use of PMDs both pleasant and safe.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: At its core, our public transport system will have a high capacity, highly connected and reliable public train system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The expansion of our rail system is on track.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will soon select and appoint the operator for the Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have begun to call tenders for Circle Line Stage 6.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have started planning for the Jurong Region and Cross Island Lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I will be one of those eight in 10.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We particularly look forward to the opening of Downtown Line 3.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It will be a game-changer for residents living in the east, just as Downtown Line 2 was for the west and north-west residents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: A recent study found that one out of six rides on the Downtown Line was made using new EZ-Link cards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This suggests that a sizeable number of commuters, perhaps living along the Bukit Timah corridor, are switching to rail.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The experience of the Downtown Line gives us confidence that a car-lite Singapore is achievable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Over at Bukit Gombak, Mayor Low Yen Ling has called for Hume MRT station to be opened.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The long-term development of that precinct, including the upcoming Rail Corridor development, can justify an MRT station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is why we have made provision for it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: However, the pace of development will determine the timing for the opening of the station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As soon as there is sufficient ridership justification, we shall open the MRT station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng observed that train reliability is improving.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Indeed, it is, although we are not yet where we want to be.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As he noted, we have an objective measure called the Mean Kilometres Between Failure (MKBF) to track our progress objectively.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our MKBF crossed 160,000 train-km in the first half of last year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And next year, we will shoot for 400,000.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As I previously explained to Mr Dennis Tan in this House, raising train reliability is a multi-year effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It takes years because replacement of ageing assets takes years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This year, we will replace the old third rail system which had been causing some problems to the East-West Line recently.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will soon complete the upgrading of the signalling system for the North-South Line, which will bring a lot of benefits to many residents, including the residents of my favourite Member of Parliament, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Next year, we will do the same for the East-West Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Getting it done perfectly, flawlessly, is almost impossible.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That has been the painful experience of London, Hong Kong and Taipei.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They warned us that we should expect many teething problems when we cut over the signalling system to the new one this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, I am all mentally prepared for criticisms from Er Dr Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will do our best to minimise inconvenience, but be prepared for some hitches.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng highlighted the recent hitches between Jurong East and Joo Koon stations on the East-West Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have very old signalling components there which need replacement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But, sometimes, maintenance and replacement works cannot be completed during the limited engineering hours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is why train service for that stretch was occasionally impacted when planned works extended into revenue hours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I have heard Mr Ang's suggestion and I shall ask LTA and SMRT to consider ending the revenue service for that stretch of the East-West Line earlier so that we have more engineering hours for these works.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, we have completed the transition of SMRT Trains to the New Rail Financing Framework (NRFF).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We took ownership of SMRT's rail assets last October, and Temasek's delisting of SMRT also allows it to focus on its core responsibility without the short-term pressures of being a listed company.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It took us many years and I am glad that we have now completed it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And it will not be just a mere one-for-one replacement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will, in the process, upgrade the trains as well as the power supply system to tap on new technology which is now available.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For the North East Line, we are also working with SBST to refurbish and upgrade their first-generation trains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked if we can do predictive maintenance for our trains and tracks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Indeed, predictive maintenance is the way to go.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are acquiring the necessary tools and capabilities for this purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These include new generation automatic track inspection systems and condition monitoring tools for real-time data collection and analysis.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I also hear Mr Zaqy's concern about the noise generated from passing trains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are aligned with the NEA on what is the acceptable level of noise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are closely monitoring the situation and are implementing system-wide noise mitigation measures.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our trains have noise-dampening wheels and our operators are servicing the train wheels and tracks more frequently.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is, however, a major multi-year programme, as we have to coordinate it closely with so many other maintenance, improvement and upgrading works that compete for precious engineering hours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The improvement has been felt on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I appreciate Mayor Low Yen Ling's feedback on new bus services in Bukit Gombak.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But I know that we can never do enough.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I have heard her call for better connectivity to the upcoming Community Club in Bukit Gombak.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: She is a very good Member of Parliament and I have a soft spot for good Members.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Another good Member is Er Dr Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I have also heard her feedback on Services 811 and 860, and for more covered linkways.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will see what else we can do.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But let me also plead and seek Members' understanding that, for financial prudence, bus service provisions require a minimum ridership.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If ridership goes down as commuters switch to rail, we will have to remove or amend existing bus services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Otherwise, you will have half-empty buses running on the roads causing pollution and it is also a waste of taxpayers' money.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, our bus infrastructure has expanded in tandem with the larger bus fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have now three new interchanges and more parking lots at existing interchanges.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But, critically, we have moved all the bus operators to the Bus Contracting Model, with LTA taking over bus assets and infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is another major transformation in the transport sector and for the bus industry.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I was looking at the bids and it has attracted very competitive bids, with lower prices, on average, compared to the previous two tenders.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Later this year, we will call the tender for our fourth package at Bukit Merah.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: With competition, bus operators are working harder to improve their service.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As Mr Melvin Yong pointed out, our bus captains are the key to delivering higher service levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our bus captains strive to improve bus arrival regularity and reduce bunching − a very big complaint from the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA has set fair but ambitious standards, and our bus captains are working closely with their service controllers to manage bus arrivals real-time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is why, sometimes, some buses on certain routes have to be driven very slowly.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is because they want to arrive punctually, as scheduled, because road conditions can vary during the day.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And this is the only way to solve the bunching problem.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If you want the bus drivers to drive as fast as the roads can take, then sometimes they may arrive too early and there will be complaints about bunching.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But I accept that this is still a new system, both for regulators as well as the regulatee, and we shall see how else we can calibrate the system to make it work better for us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But it has worked very well elsewhere − London, Australian cities − and I see no reason why it cannot work here, too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As our public transport system improves and expands, fewer people will need to own a car.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, the various vehicle control policies, like COE and ERP, remain relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But from time to time, we refine them as circumstances change.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And one big move we made this year is to stop the contribution of motorcycle COEs to the Open Category.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Very few motorcycles have been registered under Category E COEs due to the high Category E premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This recent move will stabilise the motorcycle population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is in response to many Members' and motorcyclists' as well as the Chambers of Commerce's concerns that the motorcycle population is shrinking.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Another move is to improve the progressivity of the vehicle tax system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In 2013, we introduced the tiered ARF for cars, taxis and commercial vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, this year, we extended the same to motorcycles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA's dialogues with them are at least twice a year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Both ideas came up from the industry in the process of brainstorming and we are happy to be able to implement them this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As I have said, the Singapore Motorcycle Trade Association is an important stakeholder and is our partner.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Other than market-sensitive information, we share with them as much as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Henry Kwek voiced the challenges faced by businesses and we are mindful of their difficulties.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As for Euro 6 emission standards, these are regulated by my colleague in MEWR.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We did discuss in Cabinet and the intention to move it to Euro 6 next year, having served the industry notice since 2014, I think there is sufficient time for the industry to respond.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I know there are some concerns about whether there would be enough vehicles, Euro 5, and some questions on why can we not go to Euro 5 first, and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Having decided on Euro 6, I think we should just move.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The market has enough Euro 5 vehicles and models to meet the demand.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources will share more details later.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: My own take on this issue is this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Europe's embrace of diesel vehicles has now made many cities highly pollutive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is a sad case of unethical commercial practices making money at the expense of public health.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They are now trying to reverse the trend.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Paris, Madrid, Athens and Mexico City have all announced that they will ban diesel vehicles from their city centres, latest by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I think we, too, should nudge down the population of diesel vehicles and work towards becoming a diesel-free city.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The restructuring of the diesel tax should be read in that context.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Under the new Bus Contracting Model, the Government is now responsible for buying and replacing buses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We pay bus operators a fee to run the bus services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Although fare revenue goes to the Government, it is not enough to cover operating costs and the Government has to top up the deficit.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Similarly, with the transition to the New Rail Financing Framework, the Government is now responsible for replacing rail assets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And over the next five years, we also expect to spend $4 billion on rail.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And all this − $4 billion plus $4 billion equals $8 billion − is on top of the about $20 billion we will be spending to build new public transport infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We must ensure that the fiscal burden does not become too excessive for taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In the earlier years, I remember, as a young officer in the Civil Service, our objective was to split the responsibility in transport by having taxpayers pay for the construction of the infrastructure, in other words, capital expenditure (capex) − the Government and the taxpayers pay for it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But commuters must bear the operating costs through transport fares.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In other words, transport fares must be able to cover the operating costs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But over the years, as fares have not kept up with rising costs, taxpayers have to subsidise more and more of the operating costs, especially as we have been raising service standards significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: While the Government will continue subsidising public transport heavily, we must find a fair balance in the relative burden to be borne by commuters, taxpayers and operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Fares are regulated by the independent Public Transport Council (PTC), through a multi-year fare formula.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The current fare formula will expire after this year's fare exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am confident that they will decide wisely.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Last year, they took a big step to standardise the train fares across all MRT lines and no longer make a distinction between above-ground and underground lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As a regular user of the Circle Line with a Senior Citizen card, I see my fare reduced from 92 cents to 87 cents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But remember: the PTC cannot always bring good news; sometimes, they have to adjust fares upwards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: When they do, I hope commuters will be understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: A good transport system connects people to places and also connects people with one another.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Public transport is a common space where we interact with fellow Singaporeans and where collective memories are made.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, let us shape this common space together to raise our quality of life and make Singapore among the most liveable cities in the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Also, many asked if they will be hit with a double whammy now that LTA has just relaxed earlier this year the requirements for taxi availability.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: How can the Ministry ensure that the public will be adequately served?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: From a regulatory point of view, there are many possibilities for transport in the near future and I think the Minister just now covered some of these, such as autonomous vehicles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must look at both the economic and social impact shifts in the transport paradigm; and what this means for commuters and Singaporeans whose rice bowls could be impacted, such as autonomous vehicles and other aspects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, today, you find taxi drivers being impacted, too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On a more national strategic consideration, I would like to ask the Ministry how our sea and air ports will be differentiating themselves, with growing competition from the region, be it the new Malaysian port or the Kra Canal development.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What new strategies and features will be put in place to ensure the continued attractiveness of our ports?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I look forward to hearing from the Minister on these considerations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Chairman, the high number of unhired taxis and rental cars is worrying.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: To compete, taxi operators are introducing the dynamic pricing model.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What is the way forward to balance traditional taxis and new market players?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, we have two pilot programmes for driverless vehicles running.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on our future plans for driverless cars and buses?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What kind of future is there for today's drivers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: But as Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union, I am equally concerned with the possible implications on some 50,000 workers who drive for a living.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Many of these drivers − bus captains, truck drivers and taxi drivers − are middle aged and are not highly educated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How can we help them transition into a driverless world?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: What is the projected implementation timeline for autonomous vehicles in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can the Ministry work closely with the union on methods and pace of implementation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How can we leverage the Singapore Bus Academy to upskill and multi-skill our bus drivers for future jobs and not just basic training for current jobs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles may be a decade away.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, only about half of them are actively driving a taxi.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them have commented that hiring agreements with taxi operators are cumbersome and opportunities to drive a taxi on a part-time basis are limited.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, there are more flexible hiring options, including even an hourly rental scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry, therefore, consider piloting a trial to encourage inactive TDVL holders to keep their licence and driving skills current by driving a taxi?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an incentive, the Ministry can consider reducing their licence renewal fee if they clock a stipulated minimum number of hours driving taxis on the roads within the year.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The new diesel tax does translate to additional business costs burden on taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cabbies told me that they want to be made more competitive and not to seek less competition.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, will LTA consider reviewing the overall business operating costs of the taxi business, to seek new and effective ways to manage rental costs incurred by drivers, especially since they are also facing intense competition from private hire car drivers as well?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are two areas I wish to highlight for further review.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the space available on buses for wheelchairs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While certainly welcome, the fact is that the number of wheelchairs that a bus can accommodate is very limited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have received feedback from disabled persons living in a charitable home about the difficulties posed when a few wheelchair-bound persons need to travel at the same time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Due to the limited space on board, they would need to board the buses in turn and wait at their destinations for subsequent buses carrying their friends to arrive, greatly increasing their travelling time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should a contingency arise, say, in the MRT system that requires evacuation or diversion of passengers, do our emergency plans spell out how we will communicate and protect those who are physically or mentally impaired, including the wheelchair-bound or those impaired in vision or hearing?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To what extent have such plans been exercised?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While there are merits to the Silver Zone initiative, there are also safety concerns and operation as issues that need to be resolved.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: First, the implementation of the Silver Zone programme must go hand-in-hand with the widening of the pedestrian footpaths in the area.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is because the roads in the Silver Zone will be narrowed substantially to slow down traffic in the area.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will leave very little room for cyclists to manoeuvre.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As some pinch points along Hougang Avenue 5 are designated Silver Zones, there is virtually no room for cyclists and buses to co-exist.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Due to safety concerns, cyclists may take to the footpath and this will create another set of problems.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The elderly, expectant mothers and young children are all at risk when cyclists are forced to share footpaths that are not designed to be shared in the first place.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Without the widening of the pedestrian footpath for Silver Zone, it is an accident waiting to happen, either on the narrow road or on the narrow footpath.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Second, the courtesy crossing is probably one of the most misunderstood features of the Silver Zone initiative.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some courtesy crossings are designed to look like zebra crossings without the white stripes and light poles.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In fact, when the Silver Zone was done up in Hougang, a few residents told me the contractors forgot to pain the white stripes and left.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Who is supposed to show courtesy at such crossing − the pedestrian or the motorist?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: According to LTA, it is the responsibility of the pedestrian to keep a look-out for on-coming vehicles at such crossings.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have seen motorists stopping for pedestrians to cross, while others did not.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is made more confusing when motorists have to slow down at such crossings due to the pinch points and the elevated crossing, but they may not have the intention to stop for pedestrians to cross.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, motorists may show courtesy on one side of the road while, on the other side, they may not.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How would the pedestrians know who will stop for them?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There is too much second-guessing at courtesy crossings, and that is a recipe for accidents to happen.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The term "courtesy crossing" is a misnomer to begin with because there is no change to the way pedestrians are supposed to cross the road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We look left, look right and look left again before we make a judgement call to cross the road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The pedestrians still have to stop for vehicles to pass.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, what is this added courtesy all about?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The safety concerns for cyclists and pedestrians over the narrow footpaths can be easily addressed.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The confusion over the courtesy crossing, however, needs to be addressed sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Residents have shared incidents of near-misses at such crossings and I hope LTA will look into resolving this confusion soon.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Electric vehicles are seen as a solution to this problem and some are promoting it as a game-changing growth industry, especially if it is coupled with self-driving technology in the near future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The electric car-sharing scheme that is being rolled out this year is an excellent programme in terms of scale and scope.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fact that the public can use up to 20% of the 2,000 charging points is a good move to encourage private electric car ownership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: LTA announced in August last year that Go-Ahead Singapore was putting an e-bus on a six-month trial.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Allowing shared use of footpaths may invariably increase the risk of accidents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Besides suitable sign-posting, footpaths should always be sufficiently wide to allow for such safe shared use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Last year, I filed a Parliamentary Question asking the Minister about the recommended width for footpaths and whether the Ministry will conduct an island-wide review to ensure that existing footpaths which are often used by cyclists are widened in accordance with the minimum width.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I assume the Minister meant that 1.5 metres is the "recommended" width.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In reality, there are some footpaths which are often used by both cyclists and pedestrians which may be narrower than 1.5 metres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This footpath is heavily used by cyclists and PMD users travelling between Bedok and the industrial estate, as well as pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Some residents have shared with me during my house visits that there is a dangerous choke-point at the location around the bus stop where the footpath connects to the staircase leading to Block 95, right by the bus stop.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Coming from the direction of the industrial estate, the footpath curls left round the back of the bus stop, effectively creating a dangerous blind spot made worse by the advertisement billboard which obstructs the view of both cyclists and people at the bus stop.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I urge the Ministry to carefully review the width of all footpaths which are often used by cyclists or PMD users, to ensure the safety of all users.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I understand and accept that these devices would allow more people, especially the elderly, to move around without the use of the car.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will be environmentally friendlier and help Singapore achieve a car-lite society faster.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, members of the public have given feedback that they are still worried about the potential for accidents on the footpaths caused by reckless and inconsiderate users of such powered mobility devices or power-assisted bicycles.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The concern is really for the young children and the elderly who are less alert to the dangers of speeding riders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge LTA to have a greater outreach to all potential riders of powered mobility devices or power-assisted bicycles so that they can learn to be considerate and responsible riders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: LTA should conduct safety courses not just in English but also in other languages for riders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If LTA anticipates that more seniors will be using such devices, LTA should conduct such safety courses in the vernacular languages and at convenient places like the Community Centres or Community Clubs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We need to do more to reach out to the potential riders so that they can learn to respect other road and public path users.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In many parts of Europe and Australia, both pedestrians and riders of powered devices are able to co-exist because of mutual respect and consideration for each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also call on LTA to enlarge its team of enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Without adequate enforcement, there is a real risk that riders may simply ignore the LTA rules and ride recklessly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the process, they endanger other road or footpath users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: To make our city bicycle-friendly will entail building cycling infrastructure, extensive cycling paths that are clearly marked out, and putting up signages.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: With our cycling tracks gradually getting more crowded because they are popular with more cyclists and PMD users, we all need to do more to promote a cycling culture and inculcate a mindset for all on safety and etiquette, such as giving way to cyclists, road users and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: As Minister Khaw mentioned earlier, Ang Mo Kio has completed Phase 1 of its dedicated cycling path project.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I wonder if his Ministry has an initial assessment of its effectiveness and what lessons have we learnt from this project.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: The national bicycle-sharing scheme to be piloted in some areas by year-end is another good initiative.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Will the Ministry consider extending this scheme to Ang Mo Kio as well?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: The necessary infrastructure is already in place to support the rolling out of such a scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Apart from the national bicycle-sharing scheme, other privately operated schemes are also in play.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Are there plans to have more of these schemes ply other parts of the island which are not covered in the pilot trial of the national bicycle-sharing scheme?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: And what concerns will the Ministry have with regard to these privately run schemes?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: In addition, how would the privately run bicycle-sharing scheme be addressing safety concerns?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: For example, how will the users' minimum age be ascertained should they participate in the bicycle-sharing scheme and use it on the roads?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Beyond bicycle-sharing, can we also push for greater inclusiveness and more efficient use of resources?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Can we allow for the cycling infrastructure, such as docking stations and smart locks systems, be extended to other private bicycles and PMDs not on the national bicycle-sharing scheme as well?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Three companies − Ofo, Mobike and Bluegogo − dominated the market.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: They provided thousands of bicycles for rental and the rental fee started from as low as 10 cents RMB per ride.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: These rented bicycles were parked all over the places haphazardly on the pedestrian pavements.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Ofo and Mobike, which are known as Obike in Singapore, have started operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Ofo charges as low as 50 cents per ride in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The rate is very competitive, attractive and affordable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Last Sunday, when I was in my constituency, I had the chance to try the use of an Obike.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It was left behind at a void deck in Jurong West.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, I used the Obike app to unlock the bicycle and tried riding it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I was even given a $3 credit when I registered online.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: From the Obike app, I could see that the yellow rental bicycles were in abundance in availability in the nearby blocks as well as at the Lakeside MRT station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Ofo and Obike have indicated that they will push out a few thousand bicycles over the next few months without the need for fixed docking stations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It appears that the services provided by these two innovative companies could help fix the first- and last-mile problem of connecting commuters to and from MRT stations.
